zh: 第三、釋事世間者，此據得初禪時獲六神通，見世諦事，了了分明，如觀掌內菴摩勒果。此則現覩眾事，不同上說，以義比類，惟忖分別世事也。今就明事世間內，亦為二意：第一、正見事世間相；第二、釋成覺觀五支義。今釋第一、事世諦相者，上根行人福德智慧利故，證初禪時，有二因緣得五神通：一者、自發；二者、修得。
en: Third, explaining the world of witnessed phenomena: this is based on obtaining the six supernormal powers upon attaining the first dhyāna, seeing the phenomena of conventional truth with utter clarity, like observing an āmalaka fruit resting in the palm of one's hand. This, then, is a matter of directly witnessing the manifold phenomena themselves, unlike what was explained above, which proceeded by analogical reasoning from sense, inferring and distinguishing worldly affairs through comparison alone. Now, in clarifying the world of witnessed phenomena, this too has two aspects: first, directly seeing the mark of the world of witnessed phenomena; second, explaining how the five factors of initial thought and the rest come to completion.

Now, explaining the first, the mark of the conventional truth of witnessed phenomena: for a practitioner of superior faculty, whose merit and wisdom are sharp, upon realizing the first dhyāna, there are two causes and conditions by which the five supernormal powers are obtained — first, spontaneous arising; second, cultivated attainment.

zh: 一、自發者，是人入初禪時，深觀根本世間三事，即能通達義世間相。覺義世諦時，三昧、智慧轉更深利，神通即發，更得色界四大清淨造色眼成就。以此淨色之心眼徹見十方一切之色，事相分明，分別不亂，名天眼通。所餘天耳、他心、宿命、身通亦復如是。得五通故，明見十方三世色心境界差別不同，眾生種類、國土相貌，一一有異，是為異見事世間也。故經言：「深修禪定，得五神通。」
en: First, spontaneous arising: when this person enters the first dhyāna, deeply contemplating the three matters of the root world, one thereby becomes able to penetrate the mark of the world of meaning directly. As one perceives the conventional truth of meaning, samādhi and wisdom turn ever more deeply sharp, and the supernormal powers thereupon arise of themselves — one further attains the accomplishment of the form realm's four elements as pure derived matter, forming the eye. Through this eye of the pure-matter mind, one sees through, in every direction, all form whatsoever — its mark distinct, one's discrimination unconfused — and this is named the heavenly eye. The remaining powers — the heavenly ear, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, and the power over the body — are likewise obtained in just this way. Having obtained these five powers, one clearly sees, throughout every direction and the three times, the differing realms of form and mind, the manifold kinds of sentient beings, and the countless features of every land, each and every one distinct from the rest — this is directly witnessing the differentiated marks of the world of witnessed phenomena. Hence the sutra says: "Deeply cultivating dhyāna concentration, one obtains the five supernormal powers."

zh: 第二、修得。五通見事世間者，如《大集經》言：「法行比丘獲得初禪，入禪已，欲得身通，繫心鼻端，觀息入出，深見九萬九千毛孔息之出入，見身悉空，乃至四大亦復如是。如是觀已，遠離色相，獲得身通，乃至四禪亦復如是。云何法行比丘獲得眼通？若有比丘得初禪，觀息出入，真實見色。既見色已，作是思惟：如我所見三世諸色，意欲得見，隨意即見，乃至四禪亦復如是。云何法行比丘得天耳通？憍陳如！若有比丘得初禪，觀息出入，次第觀聲，乃至四禪亦復如是。云何法行比丘得他心智通？若有比丘觀息出入，得初禪時，修奢摩他、毘婆舍那，是名他心智，乃至四禪亦復如是。云何法行比丘得宿命智？憍陳如！若有比丘觀出入息，得初禪時，即獲眼通。獲眼通已，觀於初有歌羅邏時，乃至五陰生滅，乃至四禪亦復如是。」既得五通，即能見十方三世、九道聖凡眾生種類、國土，所有一一相貌差別不同，是名修得神通，見事世間通達無閡。
en: Second, cultivated attainment. As for seeing the world of witnessed phenomena through the five cultivated powers, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: "The dharma-practicing monk, having obtained the first dhyāna, once entered into dhyāna and wishing to obtain the power over the body, fixes the mind at the tip of the nose, contemplating the breath entering and going out, deeply seeing the breath entering and going out through ninety-nine thousand pores, and seeing that the body is, throughout, empty — and, further still, that the four elements are likewise so. Having contemplated in this way, one grows distant from the mark of form and thereby obtains the power over the body — and, further still, this holds true all the way through the fourth dhyāna as well.

"How does the dharma-practicing monk obtain the eye-power? Should a monk who has obtained the first dhyāna contemplate the breath entering and going out, he truly sees form. Having seen form in this way, he reflects thus: whatever form throughout the three times I now see, wishing to see it, I see it exactly as I wish — and, further still, this holds true all the way through the fourth dhyāna as well.

"How does the dharma-practicing monk obtain the heavenly ear? Kauṇḍinya! Should a monk who has obtained the first dhyāna contemplate the breath entering and going out, and, in due order, contemplate sound — further still, this holds true all the way through the fourth dhyāna as well.

"How does the dharma-practicing monk obtain the wisdom-knowledge of others' minds? Should a monk contemplate the breath entering and going out and, upon obtaining the first dhyāna, cultivate calming and insight, this is named the wisdom-knowledge of others' minds — and, further still, this holds true all the way through the fourth dhyāna as well.

"How does the dharma-practicing monk obtain knowledge of past lives? Kauṇḍinya! Should a monk who contemplates the breath entering and going out, upon obtaining the first dhyāna, thereupon obtain the eye-power. Having obtained the eye-power, he observes the time of the first kalala-stage, and, further still, the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates — and, further still, this holds true all the way through the fourth dhyāna as well."

Having obtained these five powers, one is thereupon able to see, throughout the three times and every direction, the manifold kinds of beings — noble and ordinary alike — across the nine realms of existence, and every land, each and every feature differing from the rest. This is named the cultivated attainment of the supernormal powers, penetrating the world of witnessed phenomena without any obstruction whatsoever.

zh: 第二、次釋成覺觀五支義。今先釋覺，亦為三義：一、下；二、中；三、上。下覺、大覺者，用天眼通徹見諸色分別，眾生種類非一，國土所有差別不同，名字亦異，故名為覺也。大覺者，即覺世間所有但假施設，諦觀四大，即不見有世間差別之異，了了分明，故名大覺。餘四通亦爾。第二、明次品覺、大覺者，用天眼通見四大色，即知其性各異，故名為覺。知四大無常生滅，性無差別，故名大覺。餘四通亦爾。第三、明上品覺、大覺者，用天眼通明見無常之法八相有異，是名為覺。覺知八相之法本來空寂，一相無相，故名大覺。餘四通亦爾。此則略說用五神通見事世間覺、大覺相。思惟、大思惟，觀於心性，成就覺支之相，類如前說，餘觀支、喜、安、定等，亦當如是一一分別。行者當知，若聲聞、緣覺得此禪故，依定獲得不壞解脫、無礙解脫、三明、六通，故名通明觀。若菩薩大士住此禪時，即得無礙大陀羅尼，乃至四禪亦復如是。
en: Second, next explaining how the five factors of initial thought and the rest come to completion. Here, initial thought is first explained, likewise having three senses: lower; middle; and upper.

Lower initial thought and great initial thought: through the heavenly eye's own power, seeing through and distinguishing every form directly, the kinds of sentient beings not being of a single sort, the features possessed by every land differing one from another, their very names likewise distinct — this is named initial thought. Great initial thought: perceiving that everything the world possesses is merely a provisional designation, closely contemplating the four elements, one thereby no longer sees any differentiated mark belonging to the world at all, this utterly clear and distinct — this is named great initial thought. The remaining four powers follow this same pattern.

Second, clarifying the middle grade of initial thought and great initial thought: through the heavenly eye's own power, seeing the form of the four elements, one thereby knows that their own natures each differ from one another — this is named initial thought. Knowing that the four elements are impermanent, arising and ceasing, their nature without any differentiation at all — this is named great initial thought. The remaining four powers follow this same pattern.

Third, clarifying the upper grade of initial thought and great initial thought: through the heavenly eye's own power, clearly seeing that the impermanent dharma bears the eight marks, each distinct from the rest — this is named initial thought. Perceiving that this very dharma of the eight marks is originally empty and still, a single mark that is no mark at all — this is named great initial thought. The remaining four powers follow this same pattern. This, then, briefly explains, through the five supernormal powers, the mark of initial thought and great initial thought within the world of witnessed phenomena. Deliberation and great deliberation, contemplating the nature of mind, and the accomplishment of the mark of the factor of initial thought all follow the same pattern as already given before; the remaining factors — sustained reflection, joy, ease, and concentration — should likewise, each in turn, be distinguished in this same way.

The practitioner should know: should a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha obtain this dhyāna, then, based upon this concentration, one obtains the indestructible liberation, the unobstructed liberation, the three insights, and the six supernormal powers — hence this is named the thorough-and-bright contemplation. Should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abide in this dhyāna, one thereupon obtains the unobstructed great dhāraṇī — and, further still, this holds true all the way through the fourth dhyāna as well.

The two roads to the five supernormal powers — arising spontaneously out of deepened samādhi, versus being cultivated deliberately through the breath-body-mind method — are given equal standing, and the quoted passage traces the same dharma-practicing monk (法行比丘) attaining each power in turn from a first dhyāna reached through watching the breath, all the way through the fourth dhyāna — though not by the breath alone: the heavenly ear comes by contemplating sound in sequence, knowledge of others' minds by cultivating calming and insight, and knowledge of past lives only after first obtaining the eye-power. The closing line is the payoff for the entire "thorough-and-bright contemplation" section: this is the dhyāna that gives śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas the three insights and six powers, and gives bodhisattvas the unobstructed great dhāraṇī — the same single method yielding a different fruit depending on the vehicle of the one who practices it.

items.en: The Second, Third, and Fourth Dhyānas
items.zh: 二禪 · 三禪 · 四禪

zh: 次明二禪。自此已下，乃至非想滅定禪門，轉復深妙，事相非一，寧可具辯？今但別出經文，略釋正意而已。所言二禪者，經云：「二禪者，亦為名離，亦名為具。離者，同離五蓋；具者，具足三支，謂喜、安、定。」釋曰：行者於初禪後，心患初禪覺觀動散，攝心在定，不受覺觀，亦知上地不實，諦觀息、色、心三性，一心緣內，覺觀即滅，則發內淨大喜三昧，於定內見身如泡，具二禪行。
en: Next, clarifying the second dhyāna. From here on, all the way through the dharma-gate of the concentration of cessation following neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the matter grows ever more deep and subtle, its phenomena no longer singular — how could it be treated in full? Here, only the sutra's own text shall be set out separately, its main sense explained in brief.

As for the second dhyāna, the sutra says: "The second dhyāna is likewise named departure, and likewise named completeness. Departure means departing equally from the five hindrances; completeness means being complete with three factors, namely joy, ease, and concentration." Explanation: the practitioner, after the first dhyāna, whose mind grows troubled by the first dhyāna's own initial thought and sustained reflection, agitated and scattered, gathers the mind within concentration, no longer accepting initial thought and sustained reflection, and also knows that the higher stage is not real. Closely contemplating the three natures of breath, form, and mind, the mind one-pointedly fixed within, initial thought and sustained reflection thereupon cease, and internal purity's own great joy-samādhi thereupon arises — within concentration, one sees the body as a bubble, complete with the second dhyāna's own practice.

zh: 次明三禪，經云：「三禪者，亦名為離，亦名為具。離者，同離五蓋；具者，具足五支，謂念、捨、慧、安、定。」釋曰：行者於二禪後，心患厭大喜，動散攝心不受，亦知上地不實，攝心諦觀，喜法即謝，發身樂，即於定內見身如雲，成三禪行。次明四禪相，經云：「四禪者，亦名為離，亦名為具。離者，謂同離五蓋；具者，具足四支，謂念、捨、不苦不樂、定。」釋曰：行者於三禪後，心厭患樂法，一心不受，亦知四禪非實，諦觀三性，即豁然明淨，三昧、智慧與捨俱發，心不依善，亦不附惡，正住其中，即於定內見身如影，具四禪行。
en: Next, clarifying the third dhyāna, the sutra says: "The third dhyāna is likewise named departure, and likewise named completeness. Departure means departing equally from the five hindrances; completeness means being complete with five factors, namely mindfulness, equanimity, wisdom, ease, and concentration." Explanation: the practitioner, after the second dhyāna, whose mind grows weary of the great joy, agitated and scattered, gathers the mind and no longer accepts it, and also knows that the higher stage is not real. Gathering the mind and closely contemplating, the dharma of joy thereupon withdraws, and bodily happiness arises — within concentration, one sees the body as a cloud, accomplishing the third dhyāna's own practice.

Next, clarifying the mark of the fourth dhyāna, the sutra says: "The fourth dhyāna is likewise named departure, and likewise named completeness. Departure means departing equally from the five hindrances; completeness means being complete with four factors, namely mindfulness, equanimity, neither-suffering-nor-happiness, and concentration." Explanation: the practitioner, after the third dhyāna, whose mind grows weary of the dharma of happiness, one-pointedly no longer accepting it, and also knows that the fourth dhyāna is not real. Closely contemplating the three natures, the mind thereupon opens out, bright and pure — samādhi and wisdom arise together with equanimity, the mind no longer relying upon good nor attaching to evil, abiding correctly within — within concentration, one sees the body as a shadow, complete with the fourth dhyāna's own practice.

Having spent the entire chapter so far on the first dhyāna alone — root world, world of meaning, and world of witnessed phenomena all worked out in exhaustive detail — the text now moves quickly, treating the second through fourth dhyānas with a single sutra quotation and a brief gloss apiece. The three similes for the meditator's own body across the second through fourth dhyānas form a quiet, deliberate progression toward transparency: bubble, cloud, shadow — each stage's own self-image growing less substantial than the last, anticipating the formless attainments to come, where even the shadow is left behind.

quiz.q: How does the world of phenomena differ from the previous two?
options: with the powers one sees affairs directly, like an āmalaka in the palm, unlike inference by analogy
quiz.why: With the supernormal powers obtained in the first dhyāna, one sees worldly affairs directly, like an āmalaka fruit in the palm, unlike the earlier inference by analogy.

quiz.q: By what two means does a practitioner of superior faculty obtain the five powers on realizing the first dhyāna?
quiz.why: For one of superior faculty, the five powers come by two means: arising spontaneously or attained through cultivation.

quiz.q: According to the sūtra, how does the dharma-practicing monk attain the power over the body?
options: fixing the mind at the nose-tip, watching the breath through 99,000 pores, seeing the body and elements empty, leaving form
quiz.why: He fixes the mind at the nose-tip, watches the breath through 99,000 pores, sees the body and elements as empty, and leaves the mark of form. B, C, and D are other powers.

quiz.q: What do śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, each obtain from this dhyāna?
options: the two vehicles gain indestructible and unobstructed liberation, three insights, six powers; bodhisattvas gain the unobstructed great dhāraṇī
quiz.why: Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas obtain indestructible and unobstructed liberation, the three insights, and six powers; bodhisattvas obtain the unobstructed great dhāraṇī.

quiz.q: According to the sūtra, which factors do the second, third, and fourth dhyānas have?
options: second: joy, ease, concentration; third: mindfulness, equanimity, wisdom, ease, concentration; fourth: mindfulness, equanimity, neither-pain-nor-pleasure, concentration
quiz.why: The second dhyāna has joy, ease, and concentration; the third mindfulness, equanimity, wisdom, ease, and concentration; the fourth mindfulness, equanimity, neither-suffering-nor-happiness, and concentration.

quiz.q: How is the body seen within the second, third, and fourth dhyānas?
options: second: bubble; third: cloud; fourth: shadow
quiz.why: In the second dhyāna the body is seen as a bubble, in the third as a cloud, in the fourth as a shadow; the first used the plantain and foam.
